claims.claim: In a 2024 US survey, 32% of adults said they had been bullied at work
claims.evidenceSource: Workplace Bullying Institute, 2024 WBI U.S. Workplace Bullying Survey (web page)
claims.publicationDate: 2025-04-19 (page date as returned by fetch; survey fielded 2024)
claims.supportingEvidence: Page states 'Directly bullied - 32.3% of adult Americans'. 32% is a fair rounding. A WBI search snippet also gives 32% for the full report, but the PDF could not be machine-read.
claims.confidenceRationale: Primary source retrieved. Rounding of 32.3% to 32% is acceptable.
claims.recommendedAction: Keep. Name the source in the text (the Workplace Bullying Institute's 2024 survey) and add a link, since G2 flags no source.

claims.evidenceSource: Workplace Bullying Institute 2024 survey page; 2024 Complete Report PDF
claims.supportingEvidence: The fetched survey page gives witnesses only as a count ('Indirect experience (witnesses) - 22.6 million'), not 14%. A web search result summary attributed 14% witnessed and 46% affected to the WBI full report and flyer, but I could not read the PDF (compressed, unreadable via fetch), so I did not see it myself.
claims.confidenceRationale: Plausible and reported by a search summary, but not confirmed against a text I retrieved.
claims.recommendedAction: Qualify or confirm: a human should open the 2024 Complete Report PDF at https://workplacebullying.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/2024-Complete-Report.pdf and confirm the 14% before publication. If it cannot be confirmed, remove the clause.

claims.claim: Targets face a 62% chance of losing their jobs.
claims.evidenceSource: Workplace Bullying Institute, 2024 WBI U.S. Workplace Bullying Survey (web page)
claims.supportingEvidence: Page text: 'Targets have a 62% of losing their jobs after targeting', with job loss attributed to constructive discharge (18%) and termination, transfer or voluntary resignation (25.6%). Those components do not obviously sum to 62%; I did not reconcile them.
claims.confidenceRationale: Number matches WBI's own wording. It is a self-reported survey figure and 'losing their jobs' includes voluntary resignation, which the article does not say.
claims.recommendedAction: Qualify: attribute to WBI ('by WBI's survey estimate') and note it includes people who resign. Link the source.

claims.claim: In MIT Sloan's analysis of employee reviews, toxic culture predicted attrition 10.4 times more strongly than compensation.
claims.evidenceSource: MIT Sloan Management Review, 'Toxic Culture Is Driving the Great Resignation'
claims.supportingEvidence: Article says toxic corporate culture is '10.4 times more powerful than compensation in predicting' industry-adjusted attrition. Method: SHAP values from an XGBoost model on Glassdoor-derived Culture 500 data, relative to compensation as 1x; compensation ranks 16th among topics. A figure caption words it as '10.4 times more likely', which secondary outlets misread as a probability.
claims.confidenceRationale: Primary source retrieved; the wording 'predicted ... more strongly' matches. Data is from 2021, so it is not evidence of 2026 conditions.
claims.recommendedAction: Keep, but date it (a 2021 analysis, published 2022), name MIT Sloan Management Review and link. Do not let an edit change it to 'more likely to quit'.

claims.claim: Global engagement fell to 20% in 2025, the lowest since 2020
claims.evidenceSource: Gallup, State of the Global Workplace 2026
claims.supportingEvidence: Gallup pages state 20% engaged in 2025, down from 21% in 2024 and 23% in 2023; the trend table shows 20% in 2020 as well. So 2025 equals the 2020 level rather than being below it. 'Lowest since 2020' is accurate in the sense of 'matches the 2020 low'.
claims.confidenceRationale: Gallup page text retrieved. Gallup URL slugs returned by search are inconsistent; the 20% figure appeared on more than one retrieved Gallup URL.
claims.recommendedAction: Keep. Optionally say 'equal to the lowest level since 2020'. Link the Gallup report.

claims.claim: ...a drag Gallup prices at around $10 trillion in lost productivity.
claims.evidenceSource: Gallup, State of the Global Workplace 2026 (page retrieved at the URL below)
claims.supportingEvidence: Page text: low engagement cost the world economy 'an estimated $10 trillion in lost productivity', about 9% of GDP. A secondary summary (MangoApps) words it as 'more than $10 trillion ... in 2024 alone'; I could not retrieve a primary page that fixes the year. The page https://www.gallup.com/workplace/697904/state-of-the-global-workplace.aspx did not contain the $10 trillion figure.
claims.confidenceRationale: Retrieved a Gallup page with the figure, but the URL slug is not clearly the canonical report URL and the reference year (2024 vs 2025) is unresolved. The article's 'around' hedge fits.
claims.recommendedAction: Keep with the 'around' hedge; a human should confirm the canonical Gallup URL and the reference year before linking.

claims.claim: Manager engagement just fell from 27% to 22% in a single year.
claims.evidenceSource: Gallup, State of the Global Workplace 2026
claims.supportingEvidence: Page text: manager engagement fell from 27% to 22% in 2025 and is down nine points since 2022. A different Gallup page (697904) confirms 22% for managers but not the 27% prior value.
claims.confidenceRationale: Retrieved text matches. Same URL-slug caveat as the $10 trillion row.
claims.recommendedAction: Keep. Link Gallup. Say 'global' managers, since the article's list item does not.

claims.claim: Gallup's 2026 workplace report puts it plainly: the technology works, but the bottom-line gains aren't arriving at scale.
claims.evidenceSource: Gallup, State of the Global Workplace 2026 (retrieved page text); MangoApps secondary summary
claims.supportingEvidence: What I retrieved is narrower: in US organisations using AI, 65% of workers report a positive personal productivity impact but only 12% strongly agree AI has transformed how work gets done. A secondary source paraphrases Gallup CEO Jon Clifton as saying results are not showing up in the bottom line. I found no Gallup sentence saying the technology works and gains are not arriving at scale.
claims.confidenceRationale: Direction is roughly consistent, but 'puts it plainly' presents a paraphrase as Gallup's own statement, and the retrieved AI figures are US-only.
claims.recommendedAction: Qualify and attribute: rewrite as 'Gallup found that most US workers using AI report personal productivity gains, but few say it has transformed how work gets done', with the 65% and 12% figures sourced. Remove 'puts it plainly'.

claims.claim: Top-quartile engagement is linked to 23% higher profitability
claims.supportingEvidence: Page text: the median percent difference between top-quartile and bottom-quartile business or work units was 23% in profitability. A search summary of the same page gives the dataset as 736 studies, 347 organisations, 183,806 units. The author's own source table marked this 'not re-checked'; it is now checked. I read only the first 100,000 of 128,439 characters of the fetched page, but the 23% figure was in the portion read.
claims.confidenceRationale: Primary source retrieved and number matches. The article's wording drops the comparison group: it is a median gap between top and bottom quartile units, an association, not a causal effect.
claims.recommendedAction: Qualify wording: 'business units in the top quartile of engagement had a median 23% higher profitability than those in the bottom quartile, per Gallup's 2024 meta-analysis'. Link the source.

claims.claim: the "100 Best Companies to Work For" beat their peers by 2.3% to 3.8% a year over 28 years.
claims.evidenceSource: Great Place To Work press release on the FTSE Russell analysis of the Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For, 2026 list
claims.supportingEvidence: The only 28-year figure I found: 'annualized stock return of 13.4% over the past 28 years, compared to 9.2% for the Russell 3000 Index', a 4.2 percentage point gap. Neither 2.3% nor 3.8% appears on the page. A separate search for the two figures together found no source. The author's source table has no source for this row. Other published figures differ again (a 2018 Fortune piece: 11.66% annualised; Dec 1997 to Dec 2024: 3,174% vs 907% for the Russell 1000).
claims.confidenceRationale: The claimed range has no source and does not match the one 28-year figure I retrieved. The source is the list's own producer (Great Place To Work with FTSE Russell), so it is not independent, and the benchmark is a broad index rather than 'peers'. I am not replacing the number myself.
claims.recommendedAction: Block: remove the 2.3% to 3.8% claim. If the author wants a stock-performance point, a human editor may substitute the sourced figure attributed to Great Place To Work and FTSE Russell (13.4% vs 9.2% for the Russell 3000, 28 years to 2026), or drop the sentence. Do not publish the current figures.

claims.claim: Reference to the author's earlier piece, 'The Great Corporate Unmasking', in which she wrote about the masks we wear at work.
claims.supportingEvidence: I did not search for or retrieve this piece.
claims.confidenceRationale: Self-reference to a prior publication; existence and topic not checked.
claims.recommendedAction: Qualify: author to confirm the title and topic, and add a link, or remove the reference.

claims.claim: The opening anecdote: fourteen professionals, a six-year approval process (four sign-offs, three spreadsheets), a colleague named Richard, a prototype that did in an afternoon what took eleven days, and the manager quote 'Keep asking. I'll take the heat.'
claims.evidenceSource: Author's first-person account; article states 'Names and some details have been changed.'
claims.supportingEvidence: No independent check is possible. The article discloses that details are changed.
claims.confidenceRationale: Personal narrative. Quotations are the author's recollection. The 'eleven days' and 'two of the four sign-offs never rejected anything' details are specific and rest on her word alone.
claims.recommendedAction: Attribute: keep as the author's account, with the existing disclosure. Author to confirm the figures are as she recalls them, or reword with 'about'. Separate matter: CL-009 requires consent on file for any person named; confirm Richard is a changed name.

claims.claim: An autoimmune disease is an immune system that attacks something healthy.
claims.supportingEvidence: Standard textbook definition; I did not retrieve a source for it.
claims.confidenceRationale: Low risk and used as a metaphor, but I did not confirm it against a source.
claims.recommendedAction: Qualify: keep as an analogy, no change needed; optionally cite a medical body such as NIH.

claims.claim: The person who gets attacked is usually the one who leaves.
claims.evidenceSource: Workplace Bullying Institute 2024 survey page (partial support)
claims.supportingEvidence: WBI reports high rates of job loss among targets (62%), including voluntary resignation (25.6%) and constructive discharge (18%), but I did not verify 'usually the one who leaves' as a distinct finding.
claims.confidenceRationale: Broadly consistent with WBI, but it is a generalisation stated as fact.
claims.recommendedAction: Qualify: tie to the WBI 62% figure or soften to 'often'.

claims.claim: Answers are now close to free; AI gives confident answers in seconds; AI can't notice redundant sign-offs; certainty has been commoditised; most companies bought tools and pointed them at unquestioned processes.
claims.supportingEvidence: Argument and rhetoric. 'Most companies are in this trap' is a sweeping generalisation with no data offered.
claims.confidenceRationale: Interpretive. Only the Gallup AI claim above is checkable.
claims.recommendedAction: Keep as opinion. Consider 'many companies' in place of 'most companies'.

claims.claim: I can't prove that any single Diva tanked any single share price. But I keep seeing the same pattern.
Children ask why because the world is fascinating; Divas were curious once; being right gets you promoted and being curious gets you questioned.
claims.supportingEvidence: Generalisations about psychology and careers with no research cited.
claims.confidenceRationale: Rhetorical. No study is cited or implied.
claims.recommendedAction: Keep as opinion. Do not add a research reference without a retrieved source.
